title: Baptism
hook: water poured three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word sacrament: an outward sign that does what it shows. Your line was signs that do something. Which small sign did you mean all the way? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Picture the back of a church on a Sunday afternoon. A baby in a white outfit that took three people to get onto her. Grandparents with phones up. A godmother holding a candle a little too close to her hair. The priest takes a small shell or a jug, and pours water over the baby's forehead, once, twice, three times, saying the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The baby is usually furious about it. Everyone else is smiling. Catholics believe something enormous just happened in about four seconds. Today, the first sacrament: baptism.
screen: `A BABY IN WHITE.` → `WATER, THREE TIMES.` → `FOUR SECONDS, SOMETHING ENORMOUS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo, to dip or plunge, the word you'd use for dipping cloth into dye. The first Christians were often baptized by going right under the water, and many churches still do it that way; others pour. Either way, the sign is the same: going under, coming up. Jesus himself was baptized by John in the Jordan. And at the end of Matthew's Gospel he sends his followers out with this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." That's where the three pourings and the three names come from. What do Catholics believe baptism does? The Catechism names a lot: sins washed away, a new birth as a child of God, membership in the Church, and a mark on the soul that can never be undone, which is why a person is baptized only once. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit. So Catholics call it a birth. Your first birthday is the day you came out of your mother. This is the other one. Two surprising facts. In an emergency, anyone can baptize, even someone who isn't Christian, by pouring water and saying those words with the intention of doing what the Church does. And the Catholic Church recognizes baptisms done in most other Christian churches with water and those same three names. Christians do differ on when: Catholics, Orthodox and many Protestants baptize babies, while Baptists and many others baptize only those old enough to profess faith themselves.
screen: `BAPTIZO: TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `IN THE NAME OF FATHER, SON, SPIRIT.` · `A NEW BIRTH, ONCE, FOR GOOD.` · `ANYONE CAN BAPTIZE IN AN EMERGENCY.` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your water, or someone's. Settle, and breathe. If you were baptized, you probably don't remember it. Think instead of who was there: who held you, who promised things on your behalf. If you weren't, think of a baptism you've seen, or simply of water: the first splash of a morning shower, rain on your face. Notice it. If you pray, you can thank God for the people who carried you. Later, try to find the date. The bell holds the time.
Baptism. From the Greek for dipping under. Water poured three times in the three names, and Catholics believe, a second birth. Today's word.

Your line: your first birthday. What a week: the luminous, sorrowful and glorious mysteries, the Salve Regina, one decade a day, sacrament, and now baptism. Today, find out your baptism date, or ask someone theirs. Day one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics are usually baptized as babies: the priest or deacon pours water over the head three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with godparents promising to help raise the child in the faith.

what it means: the first sacrament: water and the three names, which Catholics believe make a person a child of God, once and for good.
what a scholar hears: baptizo, to immerse; the Trinitarian formula of Matthew 28:19, and a sacrament the Catholic Church recognizes across most Christian churches.
